Recent work supports attribute-sensitive text representations, but the retrieved papers do not establish an exact 2024–2026 recipe for BERT4Rec with a title/description encoder trained entirely from scratch. [MARS (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.00702) targets multiple item attributes and complex interest matching, but uses pretrained language models. [ITS-Rec (2025)](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/9/1748) integrates text, item IDs and positional embeddings, but relies on pretrained BERT and unavailable reviews. [Q-BERT4Rec (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.02474) explores semantic fusion, quantization and several masking strategies; its multimodal, multistage design does not establish a compliant lightweight substitute.

The closest transferable objective is older: [S³-Rec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.07873) learns item–attribute and sequence–attribute relationships alongside masked-item reconstruction, reporting benefits under sparse interactions. A practical hypothesis—not a demonstrated result for this benchmark—is one BERT4Rec with a small randomly initialized word/subword encoder over titles and descriptions, learned fusion with item-ID embeddings, and an auxiliary loss predicting selected textual tokens from masked-position states. Preserve distinguishing numbers, model identifiers and short phrases rather than reducing everything to broad topics. Hide both target ID and target text at masked input positions; candidate text can participate in the jointly trained output representation. Retain [BERT4Rec’s appended-mask inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.06690), reading the final nonpadding position. Use one checkpoint and one neural scoring function per category. Textual overlap supplies possible compatibility clues, not evidence of ownership or exact suitability; any HR@10 gain requires validation.
